newsitem.title: GERMANY: German experts hail summit as new start for NATO.
newsitem.headline: German experts hail summit as new start for NATO.

text.p: Foreign policy experts in Germany said on Friday that the U.S.-Russian summit marked a great victory for the West and a new start for NATO, but warned it could cause turmoil at home for Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

Karl Lamers, foreign policy spokesman in parliament for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), welcomed the agreement between Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton at the two-day Helsinki summit as the basis for further cooperation.
He said that not all issues had been dealt with and new issues now had to be addressed, but hailed the agreement as a step forward. "NATO has begun to change fundamentally," Lamers told Reuters.

"NATO will be much better off because of this opening towards Russia. Not that Russia will be a member, although the door remains open to it, but Russia will now be bound up in NATO's decision-making process," Lamers said.
Alexander Rahr, a Russia expert at the German Foreign Policy Society, said the summit signalled an overwhelming victory for Clinton and the West.

"Russia has given up its massive resistance to NATO's eastward expansion," Rahr told Reuters. "It's a big victory for Clinton, but Yeltsin will have trouble selling the summit as a success to the military and political elite at home."
Rahr said that, while Clinton won Yeltsin's commitment to concluding a deal with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in the near future, key Russian demands had gone unheeded.

Clinton pledged that east European countries would be able to join NATO as planned after the summit. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are the leading candidates to be invited to join after an alliance summit in Madrid in July.
But Rahr said the summit did not address Russia's demand for a firm promise from the West to rule out admitting further new members to NATO from eastern Europe.

He said Russia, which bitterly opposes the expansion of the former Soviet Union's Cold War foe to territory once under the sway of the Moscow-dominated Warsaw Pact, also wanted the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to be reinforced. Rahr said this had not been addressed.
Lamers said the summit did not deal with the issue of what happens to eastern European states, such as the Baltic states, which probably join the European Union but not NATO.
"This is something that will have to be solved by strengthening European security bodies," Lamers said.
